questions.question: Two office-seeking candidates choose platforms $a_1,a_2$ simultaneously; voters with ideal points distributed by a continuous, strictly increasing CDF $F$ vote for the nearer platform (equal distance splits), the majority wins and ties are broken by a fair coin. What does the median voter theorem predict?
options: A unique Nash equilibrium with both candidates at the median $m$, where $F(m)=\tfrac{1}{2}$.
A unique Nash equilibrium with both candidates at the mean ideal point of the voters.
A unique Nash equilibrium with the candidates at the two quartiles of $F$, one on each side.
Several Nash equilibria, one for each pair of platforms symmetric around $m$.

questions.question: Two office-seeking candidates choose platforms $a_1<a_2$; voters with ideal points distributed by a continuous, strictly increasing CDF $F$ vote for the nearer platform. Candidate 1 moves her platform closer to $a_2$ but stays below it. What happens to candidate 1's vote share?
options: It falls, since she moves away from the voters on the far left.
It rises, since the midpoint between the platforms moves right.
It is unchanged, since every voter left of $a_1$ still votes for her.
It rises only if her new platform is closer to the median $m$.

questions.question: Two office-seeking candidates choose platforms $a_1,a_2$ simultaneously; voters with ideal points distributed by a continuous, strictly increasing CDF $F$ vote for the nearer platform (equal distance splits), the majority wins and ties are broken by a fair coin. With platforms $a_1<a_2$, which voters vote for candidate 1?
options: Only voters below $a_1$, to the left of her own platform
Voters below the median, exactly half the electorate
Every voter to the left of the rival platform $a_2$
All voters below the midpoint $\tfrac{a_1+a_2}{2}$ of the platforms

questions.question: Which set of assumptions does the median voter theorem use for its convergence result?
options: One policy dimension, nearest-platform voting, and voters' ideal points symmetric about the mean
One policy dimension, nearest-platform voting, and candidates who choose platforms one after the other
One policy dimension, nearest-platform voting, two office-seeking candidates, no abstention or entry
One policy dimension, two candidates who care about the policy itself, and free entry of rivals

questions.question: Two office-seeking candidates choose platforms $a_1,a_2$ simultaneously; voters with ideal points distributed by a continuous, strictly increasing CDF $F$ vote for the nearer platform (equal distance splits), the majority wins and ties are broken by a fair coin. In the equilibrium, what is each candidate's expected payoff (payoff $1$ for winning, $0$ for losing)?
options: $1$, since each candidate wins the median voter
$\tfrac{1}{2}$, since both get half the votes and the coin decides
$0$, since neither candidate gets a strict majority
$F(m)$ for candidate 1 and $1-F(m)$ for candidate 2

questions.question: Voters' ideal points on $[0,1]$ have CDF $F(x)=\sqrt x$. Two office-seeking candidates compete as in the median voter theorem. Where do both candidates locate in equilibrium?
options: $\tfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}}$

questions.question: Seven voters have ideal points $1,2,3,6,10,11,30$ on a policy line. According to the median voter result, which platform beats every other in a pairwise majority vote?

Two office-seeking candidates choose platforms in $[0,1]$; voters' ideal points are uniform on $[0,1]$, each votes for the nearer platform, the majority wins and ties are broken by a coin. Candidate 2 is at $\tfrac{1}{2}$. What vote share does candidate 1 get by locating at $0.3$?
options: $0.3$, a sure loss
$0.5$, a tie
$0.4$, a sure loss
$0.6$, a sure win

questions.question: Two office-seeking candidates choose platforms in $[0,1]$; voters' ideal points are uniform on $[0,1]$, each votes for the nearer platform, the majority wins and ties are broken by a coin. The platforms are $a_1=0.2$ and $a_2=0.6$. What are the vote shares?
options: Candidate 1 gets $0.2$, the voters left of her platform
Candidate 1 gets $0.6$ and wins the election
Each gets one half, as the median lies between them
Candidate 1 gets $0.4$, so candidate 2 wins

questions.question: Two office-seeking candidates choose platforms $a_1,a_2$ simultaneously; voters with ideal points distributed by a continuous, strictly increasing CDF $F$ vote for the nearer platform (equal distance splits), the majority wins and ties are broken by a fair coin. Candidate 2 is at the median $m$. What is candidate 1's set of best responses?
options: Every platform, since none can beat a rival at $m$
The platforms near $m$ on the side with more voters
$\{m\}$, since any other platform loses for sure
No platform, since every choice gives at most a tie

questions.question: Both office-seeking candidates locate at the median $m$ of the voters' ideal points, whose CDF $F$ is continuous and strictly increasing; each voter picks the nearer platform. Why can neither candidate gain by moving?
options: At $(m,m)$ each candidate wins outright, so no move can improve.
A move away from $m$ keeps the share at $\tfrac{1}{2}$, so nothing is gained.
Moving to $a_1<m$ gives share $F\big(\tfrac{a_1+m}{2}\big)<\tfrac{1}{2}$: a sure loss.
Any platform is a best response to $m$, so $(m,m)$ is one of many equilibria.

questions.question: In the Hotelling-Downs election model with distance-based voting and a coin for ties, both office-seeking candidates pick the same platform $a$, which differs from the median ideal point $m$. Why is this profile not a Nash equilibrium?
options: Both candidates get $\tfrac{1}{2}$, so neither can do better; it is an equilibrium.
Either candidate can move to $m$ and win outright.
It is not one, because the candidates must take different platforms.
Either candidate can move away from $m$ and gain the extreme voters.

questions.question: Two candidates who care only about winning (payoff $1$ for a win, $0$ for a loss) pick different platforms, and candidate 2 gets more than half of the votes. Voters choose the nearer platform. Why can this profile not be a Nash equilibrium?
options: Candidate 2 can move further from candidate 1 and win by a larger margin.
Candidate 1 can copy candidate 2's platform and raise her payoff from $0$ to $\tfrac{1}{2}$.
Candidate 1 cannot improve, since candidate 2 is closer to the median.
Candidate 1 can move to the mean ideal point and always win.

questions.question: Voters' ideal points on $[0,1]$ have CDF $F(x)=x^2$, so the median is $m=1/\sqrt{2}\approx0.707$. Candidate 2 is at $m$ and candidate 1 moves to $0.4$. What is candidate 1's vote share (to three decimals)?

Customers are uniform on a beach $[0,1]$ and walk to the nearest of two vendors. What is the average walking distance with both vendors at $\tfrac{1}{2}$, and with vendors at $\tfrac{1}{4}$ and $\tfrac{3}{4}$?
options: $\tfrac{1}{2}$ and $\tfrac{1}{4}$, again twice as far at the centre
$\tfrac{1}{4}$ and $\tfrac{1}{4}$, so the locations are equally good
$\tfrac{1}{8}$ and $\tfrac{1}{4}$: clustering at the centre shortens walks
$\tfrac{1}{4}$ and $\tfrac{1}{8}$, so the equilibrium doubles the walking

questions.question: Five voters have ideal points $2,3,5,8,12$ and vote for the nearer alternative. In a pairwise majority vote between the median $5$ and the mean $6$, what happens?
options: $6$ wins, since the mean represents the average voter
$5$ wins by $3$ votes to $2$
$6$ wins by $3$ votes to $2$, with voters $5$, $8$, $12$
It is a tie, since both alternatives are central

questions.question: Platforms $a_1<a_2$ sit symmetrically around the median ideal point, $\tfrac{a_1+a_2}{2}=m$, so the vote splits evenly and a coin decides. Voters' CDF $F$ is continuous and strictly increasing; candidates only want to win. Why is this not an equilibrium?
options: It is one: each gets $\tfrac{1}{2}$, and any unilateral move breaks the tie against the mover.
Candidate 1 wins outright by moving away from $a_2$, which shifts the midpoint towards $a_1$.
Candidate 2 wins outright by copying $a_1$, since she then takes all of candidate 1's voters.
Candidate 1 wins outright by moving to any point strictly between $a_1$ and $a_2$.

questions.question: The median voter theorem assumes the CDF $F$ of ideal points is continuous and strictly increasing. Suppose instead $F=\tfrac{1}{2}$ on a whole stretch $[0.4,0.6]$ containing no voters. What goes wrong with the conclusion?
options: Every point of $[0.4,0.6]$ is a median, and uniqueness of the equilibrium fails.
Nothing: the candidates still converge to the single median $0.5$, the midpoint of the stretch.
No equilibrium exists, since a flat stretch of $F$ leaves the median undefined.
The candidates now locate at the mean of the ideal points instead of at the median.

questions.question: Voters' ideal points on $[0,1]$ have CDF $F(x)=x^2$, median $m=1/\sqrt{2}\approx0.707$. Candidate 2 is at $0.5$. Which platforms let candidate 1 win outright?
options: Platforms in $(0.5,m)$ only, stopping at the median $0.707$
Only $m\approx0.707$ itself
Every platform strictly above $0.5$
Those strictly between $0.5$ and $2m-0.5\approx0.914$

questions.question: Voters' ideal points are uniform on $[0,1]$ and each votes for the nearest platform. Three office-seeking candidates stand at $\tfrac{1}{2}$; the candidate with the most votes wins (ties by lot). Can one of them gain by moving to $0.45$?
options: Yes: she gets $0.475$ while the others split $0.525$, so she wins outright.
No: her share is $F(0.475)<\tfrac{1}{2}$, a sure loss as with two candidates.
No: each candidate gets $\tfrac{1}{3}$, and no platform can give more than $\tfrac{1}{3}$.
Yes: she gets exactly $\tfrac{1}{2}$ and wins the coin toss.
